en: Verses on the Emergence of the Three Teachings, with Commentary by Zongxiao based on the Exegesis of Shiming Shizhi.
Regarding these verses, they have been circulated from ancient times, yet the author of the original composition remains unknown. To investigate the origins of the sages of the three teachings:
Appearing in the world, he was truly the sovereign of all emperors and personages, the master of the Way of governance.
If the Sage had not appeared, how could later generations have known where to turn? The final chapter says: "The tripod is divided into three legs, yet returns to one.
If this statement is true, then the Way of the Three Teachings is fully contained therein. Upon reading the *Wen Zhongzi*, it is said: [as follows].

The flourishing of the Odes and the Documents did not prevent Qin from destroying them; this was not the fault of Confucius. The growth of the metaphysical and the profound did not prevent the Jin house from falling into chaos;
this was not the fault of Laozi and Zhuangzi. The observance of fasting and purification did not prevent the Liang state from perishing;

this was not the fault of Śākyamuni. Does the *I Ching* not say: "If it is not the right person, the Way will not be practiced in vain"? By examining the *Huangji Danglun*, one knows that regarding the Three Teachings...

This single verse expresses the utmost sincerity and corresponds with what has been communicated to the King; readers should examine it for themselves, for its essence certainly does not reside in the words alone.
Yet, regarding the rise of the Three Teachings, there are dates and years that can be verified and spiritual portents that can be attested to;
none fail to be corroborated by the classics and histories. Who could fail to observe this when viewing these records together? Thus, the words are recorded here.
This work briefly summarizes the essential meaning while comprehensively encompassing its scope;

having previously evaluated its excellence, I now further verify it against the facts and provide annotations, hoping thereby to bring forth the manifest transformations of the former sages. Should there be anything that is not so, I shall correct it accordingly.
This preface was written on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the year of Xinyou, the first year of the JiaTai era, at Zhiguangzhai in Nanh Lake.
Śākyamuni descended his traces at Kapilavastu during the twenty-fourth year of the Jia-yin cycle of King Zhao of Zhou.
Our Great Master Buddha has long since realized the wondrous body of Vairocana, which is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;

yet, by the power of his great compassionate vows, he descended his traces in Central India to manifest the appearance of recent attainment. This is what is meant: birth and extinction pertain to phenomena, and certainly do not pertain to the [Ultimate] Self.

It is thus; the accounts of his descent and birth are recorded in great detail in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras. For now, let us clarify this by relying on the Hīnayāna sources. The *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* states:
"The Bodhisattva has cultivated the Way for ninety-one kalpas and is destined to occupy the position of the 'One Life Remaining' (ekajātipratibaddha) in Tuṣita Heaven.
When the appointed time arrives, he will descend to be born as a Buddha. Thereupon, he manifested his traces in Kapilavastu.
In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, the father was named Śuddhodana and the mother was named Māyādevī. Kapilavastu is the center of three thousand suns and moons and twelve thousand heavens and earths.

When the Bodhisattva first descended to manifest his transformation, he mounted a white elephant—the essence of the piercing sun—and entered his mother’s right side while she was napping during the day.
Upon waking from her dream, she immediately knew that she was pregnant, understanding the causes and conditions thereof.

The Sūtra says: When the Bodhisattva had completed ten months in the womb, on the eighth day of the fourth month at the time of sunrise, while Māyā was in the Lumbinī Garden, the eight classes of devas and nāgas filled the void.
In the garden stood an Aśoka tree with flourishing branches and leaves; Māyā grasped a branch of the tree, and the Prince gradually emerged from her right side.
Seven stalks of lotuses sprang from the earth and fell upon him; without needing support, he walked seven paces by himself, raised his right hand, and said:
"Among all devas and humans, I am the most honored and supreme.
At that time, thirty-two auspicious omens descended from heaven, and the Four Heavenly Kings received the Prince’s body with celestial silks and placed him upon them.
Śakra held a jeweled canopy and Brahmā held a fly-whisk as they stood in attendance at his left and right;
Nanda and other nāgas emitted pure water to bathe his body, which radiated great light that illuminated the entire world.

From the time he appeared in the world until he reached the age of nineteen, he left the city to renounce the household life, practiced austerities for six years, traveled for five years, and attained enlightenment at thirty.
The body of the Unsurpassed Way constantly manifests as sixteen feet tall, with golden radiance extending one fathom and a halo of one *xiún*.
It is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings across more than three hundred assemblies.

Beginning from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and ending at the Twin Trees, there is neither small nor great being who does not return to the Buddha-realm. This is truly what is meant by "hanging the sun and moon over the dark paths" and "harnessing the carriage."
The Compassionate One sails upon the sea of suffering. However, regarding the Buddha’s birth in the Western Regions, the sūtras do not mention the year;
they simply state it was the eighth day of the fourth month. When this land [China] calculated it, the results varied and were not uniform.
Of these, the era of King Zhao of Zhou has been taken as the definitive date. Thus, the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou) states: "King Zhao Xua of Zhou ascended the throne."
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year, the Jia-yin year (the fourth month of the Zhou dynasty corresponds to the second month of the present calendar;

as will be noted below, the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month corresponds to the twelfth month of the present calendar, because the Zhou dynasty took the month of Zi as the first month of the year, which differs from the practice of the present age—this is explained in detail in the Beishan lu), the rivers and streams overflowed and the great earth shook.
That night, five-colored light and vapors entered and pierced the Great Wei constellation, pervading the western quarter.
Just as [the sky] turned blue and red, the King questioned the Grand Astrologer Suyou. Suyou reported, "A Great Sage has been born in the West;
therefore, this auspicious omen has appeared. The King asked, "What will happen to this kingdom? Suyou replied, "Nothing else;
at the end of a thousand years, his teachings and influence will reach here. The King ordered that this be engraved upon stone and buried at the South Suburban Altar of Heaven.
Previously, King Zhao personally beheld the auspicious spiritual omens of our Western Sage, yet he harbored no heart of aspiration or devotion;
that blessings and responses came as they did was surely due to the workings of destiny.
In the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, on the day of Renshen, when the Tathāgata was eighty years old, he returned to the realm of ultimate truth.
The Great Parinirvāṇa, the secret treasury of the three virtues, is named the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality);
it is the place where all Buddhas of the three periods of time, having ceased their responsive activity (*nirmāṇa*), relinquish their physical life.

Among the extensive demonstrations of the Great Hero’s deeds of manifesting extinction, none surpasses the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* translated by Faxian; thus, it says: "Once the Tathāgata had accepted the invitation of Pāpīyas..."
He said, "Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa; those who were to be delivered have all been brought to completion.

He then spoke to Ānanda, saying, "Tonight I shall enter extinction. Go to the city of Kuśinagara, between the twin śāla trees, and sprinkle and sweep the ground to make it pure, and prepare a couch for me. My body is now utterly exhausted. Ānanda received these instructions.
Weeping, they departed as the Buddha proceeded to that place, where he lay down with his head to the north and his right side toward the ground.
The fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, lining up from the earth up to the celestial realms, filling each of the four directions for thirty-two *yojanas*. All wailed and lamented in grief;
the Tathāgata then spoke again on all phenomena, finally proclaiming: "All conditioned things are impermanent; this is their nature."
"The dharma of cessation arises; when cessation has ceased, tranquility is bliss. Although I possess a vajra-body, I am not exempt from impermanence.
You all should exert yourselves with diligence and swiftly seek liberation;
this is my final instruction. The section following the cremation states: "The Tathāgata lay upon a jeweled couch amidst the śāla groves."
At midnight, he entered the fourth dhyāna, becoming silent and still, and entered parinirvāṇa.
The four pairs of eight śāla trees merged into two trees, their branches and twigs bending downward to cover him as they turned a dismal white, the color of a crane.

The great earth shook violently, and all living beings cried out in lamentation. Once he had passed into extinction, his remains were placed upon a seven-jeweled pyre according to the funeral rites for a Cakravartin King.

After a while, the coffin rose by itself and circumambulated the city of Kuśinagara seven times before entering the Perfumed Chamber. From his chest, the sacred fire flowed forth and spontaneously consumed him;
after seven days, it was exhausted. His diamond-like body was shattered into powdered *śarīra*, which the multitude collected and filled eight golden jars.
They returned to the city of Kuśinagara, erected stupas, and made offerings. The Great Sūtra states: "In the second month, the Tathāgata..."
The term "Nirvāṇa" (extinction) is like the springtime when all things are brought to life and grow, and flowers and fruits flourish and prosper.

Because sentient beings mostly harbor the notion of permanence, the Tathāgata enters extinction during this month; specifically on the fifteenth day, as the moon has neither waning nor waxing, it demonstrates the sign of being without increase or decrease upon entering Great Nirvāṇa.
The above are the teachings of the Western Regions; in this country [China], it corresponds to the period of profound tranquility.
Because this occurred during the reign of that king, the *Yiji* (Alternative Records) of the *Zhou Shu* states:
On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu (Man) of Zhou, the year of Renshen, at dawn, a violent wind suddenly arose, damaging houses and breaking trees;
the great earth, mountains, and rivers all shook. By mid-afternoon, the sky was overcast and the clouds were black, when suddenly a white rainbow appeared in the west.
Twelve rays of light pierced from north to south, remaining unextinguished throughout the night. The King questioned the Grand Astrologer Hu Duodu, who replied:
"This is the sign of decline following the passing into *nirvāṇa* of a Great Sage in the West.

When the King first ascended the throne, he had seen a stele at the Southern Suburb recording the birth of the Sage of the West; furthermore, having frequently witnessed auspicious radiance, he was apprehensive.
Since this was not appropriate for the Way of the Zhou, he commanded the Marquis of Lü to convene the feudal lords at Tushan to prepare against such calamities;

thus, there were none among them who did not receive instruction and enlightenment. As for the statement that eighty years constitute the lifespan of a Buddha, the *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) of the Tiantai School discusses this in three grades:
forty years in the lower realm, eighty years in the middle realm, and one hundred and twenty years in the upper realm.
The Buddha remained in the world for eighty years, which signifies his dwelling in the middle [of his lifespan].

If one calculates back from the year Jia-yin of King Zhao to the year Ren-shen of King Mu, the Buddha’s lifespan would have ended at seventy-nine. The figure of eighty is stated as a general approximation of the total number.
One thousand and sixteen years after the Parinirvāṇa, the Teachings were transmitted to the East during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han.

From the year *Ren-shen* of King Mu’s era when the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa, one thousand and sixteen years elapsed until the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, when the Teachings first began to be transmitted to China; thus, this is the "Inner Transmission" of the Dharma to the Han.

It is said that in the seventh year of Yongping (the *jiǎzǐ* year), during the reign of Emperor Xiaozong Xiaoming of the Later Han (Zhuang), the Emperor dreamed at night of a golden deity six feet tall, with the radiance of the sun upon its neck, flying into the palace courtyard.

Thereupon, he waited through the night until dawn and summoned his ministers to divine the meaning of the vision. (Note: Various texts state the third, sixth, or tenth year [of Yongping], while others say the seventh year; all are errors.)

During the dream, the Attendant-in-Ordinary Fu Yi submitted a memorial, stating: "Your servant has consulted the *Weizhi* (Record of Anomalies) of the Book of Zhou, as reported by the Grand Historian Suyou regarding the time of King Zhao of Zhou, which says: 'In the west, there shall appear a Great Sage whose name is Buddha;
beyond one thousand years, his voice and teachings shall reach this land. Is it not likely that what Your Majesty dreamed of must be this? The Emperor [accepted this].
Thereupon, he dispatched twelve men, including Cai Yin, a General of the Feathered Forest (Yulin Zhonglang), and the Doctors Qin Jing and Wang Zun, to seek out the matters of the dream.
Upon arriving in the country of Da Yuezhi (pronounced Zhi), they encountered the two masters Śramaṇa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the tenth year, the Dingmao year, in the Han...
The envoys returned to Luoyang, where the two monks presented the scriptures on white horses and had an audience with the Emperor.
They offered an image of Śākyamuni along with the Sanskrit manuscripts; consequently, the Baima Monastery was first established there.

By imperial decree, the image was enshrined at the Qingliang Terrace of the Southern Palace, and the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* was ordered to be translated. This [text] was then sealed away in the stone chamber of the Lantai Library.
This was the very first proclamation of the Three Jewels in the land of Han. Master Shenqing of Beishan praised it, saying:
"To borrow a dream of a single night and establish a wind of renown for ten thousand ages—those like Emperor Zhuang were truly the sovereigns of the world.
To manifest a noble mind and flourishing schemes, brilliantly inaugurating the Great Han—those like Wang Fu and Qin Cai were truly the ministers of the House of Han."
Among the Dharma-king’s remaining disciples who carry on his great legacy, there are indeed monks from India whose virtuous reputation is like that of Madhyāntika and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
How magnificent it is that the enlightened sovereign, together with two or three ministers, has promoted the teaching of the Golden Immortal (Buddhism) precisely when its customs were yet unheard of,
causing people through their sincere devotion to know where sin and merit converge, and to weary of this outflowing body while aspiring toward the Unconditioned.
The principles established for it are vast and expansive; the merits of this profound transformation cannot be fully exhausted in a single day’s discourse.
Nevertheless, from the initial emergence of the Great Dharma until the present year of *xīnyǒu*, there have been one thousand one hundred and forty-four years.
If one calculates from the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the total reaches two thousand one hundred and fifty-one years.
It has been [this many] years.
Since the Buddha was born four hundred twenty-two years ago, Laozi was born during the reign of King Ding.
The following records the times of birth for the two sages, Confucius and Laozi; since birth necessarily implies death, I have now described their lives from beginning to end.
Let those who read this not consider it redundant. According to the records, the Buddha was born in the year Jiayin of King Zhao’s reign, while Laozi was born in the year Yimao of King Xuan’s reign;
between them there were eighteen successive emperors, spanning four hundred and twenty-two years.
Furthermore, from the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until Laozi’s birth, three hundred and forty-four years had already passed.
Furthermore, although there is a tradition that Laozi departed westward across the Flowing Sands, he was separated from the Buddha by a vast distance.
The *Huahu jing* (Scripture on the Conversion of the Barbarians), which is transmitted in the world, claims that Laozi converted the barbarians to become a Buddha; is this not a fabrication?
Now, according to the *Shiji*, the *Laozi neizhuan*, the *Weishu Guochen ji*, and other sources, it is recorded that Laozi lived during the twentieth generation of the Zhou dynasty.

In the first year of the reign of Emperor Wuding (Yu), the year of Yimao (or, as some say, the third year—which is an error), on the fourteenth day of the ninth month at the hour of the Rat, he was born in Qurenli, Lixiang, Chuku County, Chen Commandery.
His father was of the Han clan, named Han Qian, courtesy name Yuanbei; his mother’s name was Jingfu.
She became pregnant after seeing the solar essence, which resembled a shooting star, fly into her mouth.
After twelve years had passed, he was born beneath a plum tree; thus, "Li" (Plum) became his surname and "Yang" (Sun) his given name.
His ears were large without lobes, and he was posthumously titled Lao Dan (The Old Man with Long Ears). He was born with a white beard and mustache, hence he was called Laozi (The Old Master).

With crane-like hair, a dragon-like countenance, a broad forehead, and a square mouth, his face was suffused with a golden hue and his tongue was patterned like brocade. He stood one zhang and two chi tall.
At forty-eight years of age, during the second year of King Jian (Yi), the year Dingchou, at twenty-three, he became an official of the Archives.
Ten years later, he was promoted to Archivist under the Pillars.
At eighty-five, in the twenty-fourth year of King Jing (Gui), the year Gengchen, seeing the decline of the Zhou virtue, he entered the Hangu Pass, where the Pass Commandant Yin Xi [met him].

Previously, Yin Xi had seen purple vapors floating over the Passes, foretelling that a person of extraordinary character would arrive. When he sought him out and found Laozi, he said with joy, "You are about to retire from the world;
will you not compel me to write a book for you? Thereupon, Laozi composed the two parts of the *Daodejing* in five thousand words, expounding the meaning of the Way and its Power.
From then on, he accompanied Xi to the shifting sands of the western frontier, where he subdued the barbarian king Fuqin.
One cannot know where the realm ends. According to the *Zhuangzi*, when Lao Dan died, Qin Shi (pronounced Tie) went to offer condolences;
he cried three times and then departed. The elders wept for him as if for their own sons, and the youths wept for him as if for their own mothers.
Master Daoist’s commentary states: "The Lord Lao descended in accordance with the times, and his passing away was serene and detached."
It is simply that he followed the principle and returned to the Truth. The *Shunzhou ji* states: "The tomb of Laozi is in Huaili, Fufeng;
this is present-day Chang'an in Yongzhou. Combining these various accounts, it is clear that Laozi never actually died;
rather, after his westward journey, he returned once more to the land of Zhou. That the *Lingbao jing* regards Laozi as a transcendent immortal is precisely what is meant by this.
The Daoist realm of Great Purity is this very teaching of the Way and its Virtue (*Dàodé*).

From the time Laozi entered the Pass until the present *xīnyǒu* year, a total of one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years have passed; as for the day of his death, it has not been recorded in the transmitted texts.
The Buddha was born four hundred and seventy-seven years before Confucius.
While the Buddha was born in the year of Jia-yin during the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, Confucius was born in the year of Geng-xu during the reign of King Ling.
Thus, the two sages were separated by four hundred and seventy-seven years. According to the "Genealogies" (Shijia) in the *Shiji*, the ancestors of the Kong clan were from the state of Song.
The fifth-generation ancestor of my family moved to the town of Zou in Changping Township, Lu State.
On the fourth day of the twelfth month in the twenty-second year of Duke Xiang of Lu—which was the twenty-first year of King Ling (Xie) of Zhou, the gengxu year—Confucius was born.
His father, Shiliang He, and his mother, Yan Wei, feared that a son might not be born in due time, and so they privately offered prayers to [the deity].
Born on Mount Nichu, his head was slightly protruding at the crown; thus he was named Qiu and styled Zhongni.
He stood nine chi and six cun tall, which the world called being a "tall man. As a child, he delighted in play, constantly arranging ritual vessels and assuming ceremonial postures.

Upon reaching adulthood, he served as an official under the Ji family, where he measured and calculated with such fairness that when he became the Superintendent of Cattle, the livestock multiplied in a single day.

He said to his uncle, "I have heard that Lao Dan is broad in knowledge of antiquity and current affairs, understands the source of ritual and music, and clarifies the ultimate destination of the Way and its Virtue;
he is my teacher. He then traveled to Zhou to inquire after him. Upon returning to Lu, his disciples increased in number.
At the age of thirty-five, Duke Zhao fled to Qi and Lu fell into chaos; thereupon [Confucius] went to Qi and served as Grand Music Master (Gao).
Zhaoshi’s subordinate official used this connection to reach Duke Jing, who wished to grant him the fields of Nixi as a fief.
Yan Ying opposed this, and the Duke was confused by his arguments. Consequently, Confucius returned to Lu at the age of forty-two.

At that time, Duke Ding had ascended the throne, and the powerful and usurping Ji clan’s minister, Yang Hu, was inciting rebellion and monopolizing the administration; therefore, Confucius withdrew from office.

Gongshe Niu rebelled against the Ji clan from Fei and summoned Confucius, wishing him to go; however, Confucius ultimately did not go. Duke Ding appointed Confucius as the Governor of Zhongdu, and within one year, the surrounding regions took him as their model.
He was subsequently appointed as the Minister of Works (Sikong) and then as the Grand Minister of Justice (Dasi kou).
After ten years, acting as Chancellor to Duke Ding, he held an audience with the Marquis of Qi at Jiaju; the people of Qi then returned the territories they had seized from Lu.
In the thirteenth year, he sent Zhong You to serve as the steward for the Ji family, leading to the demolition of the three strongholds and the collection of their armor and weapons.

The Meng family refused to demolish Cheng; they besieged it but were unsuccessful. In the fourteenth year, when Confucius was fifty-six years old, he acted as regent for the Chancellor and executed Shao Zheng-mou, thereby participating in the administration of state affairs.
The state of Lu became greatly governed. The people of Qi then presented him with female musicians and...

When Ji Zhi’s younger brother, Huanzi, received him at the border but did not present the sacrificial meat (fan) and the ritual stands (zu) to the Great Officers, [Confucius] subsequently went to Wei, staying with Yan Zhuozou, the brother-in-law of his disciple Zilu. On his way to Chen, he passed through Kuang;
the people of Kuang, taking him for Yang Hu, arrested him. Once released, he returned to Wei and stayed with Qu Boyu, where he again had an audience with Nanzi. He then departed for Song.
The disciples practiced the rites beneath a great tree; Huan Tui, wishing to kill Confucius, uprooted that tree.
He also passed through Zheng and lost his disciples there, eventually arriving in Chen where he stayed with Si Cheng Zhenzi’s family for three years before returning to Wei.
Duke Ling of Wei could not employ Confucius, so he went to where Bo Xi was serving as the governor of Zhongmou under Zhao Jianzi.
When Zizhi attacked Zhongmou, Fo Xi rebelled and sent someone to summon Confucius, but he did not go.

He was about to travel west to see Zhao Jianzi, but upon reaching the River, he turned back and stayed with Qu Boyu’s family. When Duke Ling asked about military formations, he did not answer and departed, returning once more to Chen.
When Ji Huanzi was dying, he left a final testament saying that Kangzi must certainly summon Confucius; his ministers [acted accordingly].
When Ji stopped him, Kangzi then summoned Ran Qiu. From Cai, Confucius traveled to Ye; the state of Chu sent an envoy to invite him.
As he passed through Chen and Cai on the way, those two states suspected that Chu intended to employ him.

Consequently, they mobilized their infantry and surrounded him in the wilds, cutting off his supply of grain for seven days until none could even lift their hands. Confucius nevertheless continued his recitations and studies, playing the strings and singing without ceasing. Chu—
King Zhao raised an army to welcome Confucius, intending to enfeoff him with seven hundred *li* of land organized into administrative districts (*shu-she*).
However, the Chancellor Zi Xi opposed this, and so the plan was abandoned. When Confucius returned from Chu to Wei, the Lord of Wei wished to have Confucius manage the government;
yet because Ran Qiu had distinguished himself as a general for the Ji clan during their war against Qi, the Marquis Kang summoned Confucius instead. Confucius... [text truncated]
When the Master returned to Lu, it was actually the eleventh year of Duke Ai’s reign, and Confucius was sixty-eight years old.

Although Lu ultimately did not employ Confucius, nor did Confucius seek official office; at that time, the House of Zhou was in decline, the rites and music were neglected, and the Odes and Documents were incomplete.
Thereupon, Confucius traced back the rituals of the Three Dynasties, recording the era of Yao and Shun above and [the subsequent periods] below.
Reaching the time of Duke Mu of Qin, the ancient books were transmitted; it was from Confucius that the *Liji* (Book of Rites) began.
Of the more than three thousand ancient poems, Confucius selected those suitable for application to ritual and righteousness, numbering three hundred and five pieces, to show to future generations.

Later, he took pleasure in studying the *Yi* (Changes), composing the *Tuan*, *Xiang*, and *Shuogua* commentaries. His disciples numbered approximately three thousand, many of whom were thoroughly versed in the Six Classics.

There were seventy-two men of artistic skill. In the spring of the fourteenth year of the reign of Duke Ai of Lu, while hunting in Daye, a member of the Shusun clan captured a qilin and broke its leg, regarding it as an ill omen.
Confucius said, "It is a qilin; having taken its life, my Way has reached its end.
Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals to restrain the world and apply the principles of censure and praise. When the Spring and Autumn Annals circulate, the world—
Rebellious ministers and treacherous sons were struck with fear. His disciples received the *Chunqiu*, and Confucius said, "Those who know me in future generations will do so through the *Chunqiu*;
those who condemn me will also do so through the *Chunqiu*. When Confucius was ill, Zigong requested an audience;
at that time, Confucius was leaning on his staff by the gate, singing: "The Mount Tai is collapsing! The beams and pillars are falling! The man of wisdom..."
His face grew withered and he shed tears, saying to Gong: "The Way has long been lost in the world, and none have been able to honor me as their master.
The people of Xia place the coffin on the eastern steps; the people of Zhou, on the western steps; the people of Yin, between the two pillars. I am a man of Yin.
Yesterday I dreamed that I was sitting in a state of repose between the two pillars; it seems my death is near. On the seventh day, he indeed passed away. I have examined this.

At the age of seventy-three, on the eleventh day of the fourth month at the hour of the horse (wu-shi) in the year of Renxu—the forty-second year of King Jing (Gai) of Zhou and the sixteenth year of Duke Ai of Lu—Confucius was buried. The *Jia Yu* states:
"He was buried north of the city of Lu by the Si River; the tomb did not reach the groundwater, and it was mounded in the shape of an overturned axe, its height [being such that]..."

He planted pine and cypress trees four chi high as a testament to his resolve; his disciples all observed a period of mourning for three years before departing, with the sole exception of Zigong, who dwelt in a hut at the grave for six years.
Subsequently, more than a hundred disciples and people of Lu followed him and established homes there, so that the place was named "Kong Village.
A temple was erected to enshrine his robes, cap, lute, and books, which have been preserved by his descendants from generation to generation.

In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, although he was a sovereign, he is treated with the rites due to a disciple; because he once served as a Great Officer of the State of Lu, he is titled "Master" (*fūzǐ*).
*Zhuāngzǐ* honors him as the "Empty King" (*sùwáng*). In the twenty-seventh year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, he was enfeoffed as the "King Wenxuan.
A brief account of these matters is recorded in the *Dazhong Xiangfu* [era records] of Emperor Zhenzong.

In the first year [of his reign], having returned from the eastern sacrifice at Mount Tai, he passed through Yanzhou and visited Qufu, where he entered the temple to pay his respects to the King styled Xuansheng Wenxuanwang.
Later, to avoid the taboo name of the Imperial Ancestor, the title was changed to Zhisheng (Supreme Sage) in the fifth year.
From the passing of Confucius until the present year of Xinyou, exactly one thousand six hundred and eighty years have elapsed.
"To repay the toil of life, let the young child know: / The tripod is divided into three legs, yet returns to one.

In Buddhism, beings are called *zhòngshēng* (multitudes of beings); in the Daoist school, they are called *láoshēng* (toilsome life). These names differ and their meanings differ, yet their underlying intent is the same.

"Young" (*zhì*) carries the sense of a tender grain that has not yet reached maturity. The theory of the "divided tripod" is intended to elucidate the relationship between Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism.
These three [traditions] stand together in the world; none may be omitted. To demonstrate the principle of their ultimate unity, I shall first cite various texts.
The *Laozi Xisheng jing* (The Scripture of Laozi’s Ascension to the West) states: "My teacher transformed his presence and traveled to India, skillfully entering nirvāṇa.
Fu Zi says: "The teacher of the Master of Old was named Śākyamuni. Yin Xi’s *Xisheng ji* (Record of the Ascension to the West) states: "Laozi..."
